summary.text: A neutron star is the collapsed core of a massive star, squeezed by a supernova explosion past white dwarf density to that of atomic nuclei.
It has about 1.4 times the Sun's mass in a radius of roughly 10 kilometers, making it the second-densest known class of stellar object after black holes.
Basic models say it is made almost entirely of neutrons, because extreme pressure combines electrons and protons into neutrons.

facts.label: Number in Milky Way
facts.value: Around one billion, at least several hundred million

items.prompt: Two supernova cores collapse. One ends as a neutron star and the other as a black hole. What separates them?

options.label: The black hole's core was hotter when it collapsed
The black hole's core was turning more slowly
The neutron star's leftover core is lighter than a certain limit
The neutron star's core had been larger before collapse

items.explain: A remnant with a mass above the limit becomes a black hole, because degeneracy pressure and nuclear forces cannot support it.

items.prompt: Why do newly formed neutron stars whirl so fast, much like a skater who pulls in her arms?

options.label: The core keeps most of its rotation but shrinks to a tiny radius
The supernova blast gives the core a hard push round
Its strong gravity keeps speeding the rotation up
Escaping neutrinos steadily twist the core around

items.explain: The core retains most of its angular momentum, and with only a tiny fraction of its parent's radius its moment of inertia drops sharply, so it rotates very fast.

items.prompt: Nothing inside a neutron star makes new heat. How does its surface temperature change after birth?

options.label: It stays about constant because the core stays hot
It starts very hot and steadily cools
It warms up as gravity keeps squeezing it
It cools to near zero within a few years

items.explain: New neutron stars may be ten million kelvins or more, but with no fusion they cool; even so, older cool ones are still easy to discover.

items.prompt: Neutron stars were once expected to be hard to detect because they give off so little heat. What changed that view?

options.label: Bigger telescopes could see their surfaces directly
They were found to glow brightly from ongoing fusion
They were seen pulling light out of nearby galaxies
It was found that spinning stars give off radiation

items.explain: Originally they seemed hard to detect because of low thermal emissions, but spinning stars were found to emit radiation.

items.prompt: Two neutron stars circle each other and finally merge. What do astronomers expect to detect?

options.label: Gravitational waves, plus a kilonova and a short gamma-ray burst
A steady glow of visible light from fusion, and little else
A faint radio hum that fades away within seconds
Fresh hydrogen fusion lighting up the merged star

items.explain: Merging binary neutron stars produce gravitational waves and are associated with kilonovae and short gamma-ray bursts.

items.prompt: Why would it be so hard to launch a rocket off the surface of a neutron star?

options.label: Its thick atmosphere would drag on anything rising
Its magnetic field would pull every rocket back down
Its surface is too hot for any engine to run
Its surface gravity is immense, so escape needs over half light speed

items.explain: Dense neutron stars have extremely high surface gravity and an escape velocity of over half the speed of light.
